title: The Making of the Bicycle
context:
The bicycle in its modern form is barely a century and a half old, yet it is among the most efficient machines ever built for converting human effort into movement. Its ancestor was the running machine, or draisine, invented in 1817 by the German Baron Karl von Drais. It consisted of two wheels joined by a wooden frame, and the rider pushed along the ground with his feet. The invention was prompted by a shortage of oats after a volcanic eruption in Indonesia darkened the sky and ruined harvests, making horses expensive to feed.

The next step was the addition of pedals. In the 1860s, French makers attached cranks directly to the front wheel, producing the velocipede, nicknamed the boneshaker because its wooden wheels and iron tyres made every journey uncomfortable. To travel faster, manufacturers enlarged the front wheel, since one turn of the pedals carried the rider further. This led to the penny-farthing, with a front wheel as tall as 1.5 metres. It was fast but dangerous: a rider who struck a stone could be thrown over the handlebars, and many suffered serious injuries. Despite these flaws the machines became a craze in Paris and London, and riding schools opened to teach clumsy newcomers how to stay upright.

The breakthrough came in 1885, when the English engineer John Kemp Starley introduced the Rover safety bicycle. It had two wheels of equal size and a chain that drove the rear wheel, which meant that the rider sat low and could stop with his feet on the ground. A few years later, John Boyd Dunlop reinvented the pneumatic tyre, which was filled with air and absorbed the shocks of rough roads. Together these improvements made cycling both comfortable and safe, and sales rose dramatically.

The bicycle also had social consequences. For women in the 1890s it offered a rare chance of independent travel, and campaigners such as Susan B. Anthony declared that it had done more for female emancipation than anything else. Clothing changed, as long skirts gave way to practical divided garments known as bloomers. Cyclists' clubs organised weekend excursions, and the new mobility encouraged people to marry outside their own villages, widening the pool of partners.

In the twentieth century the arrival of the motor car reduced cycling in many wealthy countries, but it remained vital in Asia and Africa, where millions of people still depend on it for work. In recent years cities have rediscovered the bicycle as a solution to congestion and pollution. Public hire schemes allow residents to pick up a bike at one station and leave it at another, and electric models with small motors are making hilly routes accessible to riders who might once have given up. The world's bicycle fleet is now estimated at well over a billion machines.
